opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about this in a few layers.

The most basic layer is that companies shouldn't be able to use contracts to silence people about risks. When I left OpenAI, there was this non-disparagement agreement tied to vested equity, and the choice was basically: sign this and keep your equity, or don't sign and lose it. I didn't sign. But the broader point is that you don't want a world where the people with the most insight into what's happening inside these companies are financially locked into silence. So step one is that non-disparagement or confidentiality agreements shouldn't be enforceable when they cover concerns about risk.

The second layer is having a legitimate channel to raise concerns. This was a big part of the "Right to Warn" letter that a bunch of us current and former employees signed. The idea is an anonymous, verifiable process where an employee can raise a concern with the board, with regulators, and with some independent organization with relevant expertise. It shouldn't just be an internal hotline that routes back to the people you're worried about. And ideally it's set up so you can share what's necessary to make the concern legible without leaking trade secrets or model weights. We're not saying everyone should be able to dump everything to the press. We're saying there should be a real path.

The third layer is protecting people who go further when those channels fail. Existing whistleblower law mostly protects you if you're reporting something illegal. But a lot of what people at AI companies might worry about isn't illegal, because there just aren't many laws on the books yet. If you think your company is about to deploy something dangerous, or cutting corners on safety evaluations, or misrepresenting its capabilities to the public, that might not be a crime. So protections need to cover good-faith disclosures about risks, not just about lawbreaking. Otherwise the law is protecting the wrong category.

And the fourth thing is culture. Even with legal protections, if raising concerns gets you quietly sidelined, passed over for promotion, or frozen out of the important projects, people learn the lesson. So companies should commit to not retaliating, and there should be some external visibility into whether that's actually honored.

Why do I care so much about this? Basically because I think we're heading into a period where a small number of people inside a few companies will know things about AI capabilities and risks that the public and governments really need to know, and know quickly. Transparency is one of the few levers that works even before we have good regulation. Whistleblower protections are kind of the backstop for transparency: if the company's official disclosures aren't honest or complete, employees are the last line of defense. You want that line to actually hold.

r001.rationale: The response proposes an anonymous channel to raise concerns with regulators and an independent organization, but does not say every employee should know they have a legal right to discuss company activities privately with designated agencies.

r002.rationale: The response identifies that existing whistleblower laws often cover only illegal conduct, but does not identify employees’ lack of awareness of existing disclosure rights as a protection gap.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I've thought about this a fair amount, partly because of my own experience leaving OpenAI and the whole non-disparagement thing. Let me try to lay out what I think the ideal would look like, and then I can say where I think the current situation falls short.

The core problem is that right now, if you're an employee at a frontier AI lab and you see something that worries you — not necessarily something illegal, but something that you think the public or the government should know about — you basically have no good options. The existing whistleblower protections in the US are mostly tied to illegal activity: securities fraud, safety violations under specific regulatory regimes, that sort of thing. But a lot of what might go wrong at an AI company isn't illegal, because there just aren't laws yet that say "you can't deploy a model that does X" or "you have to tell people if your model can do Y." So the law is sort of silent, and that means the employee is on their own.

And meanwhile, the companies have enormous leverage. You've got NDAs, you've got non-disparagement agreements — which in my case were tied to vested equity, which is a huge amount of money for most people — and you've got the simple fact that this is a small industry and everyone knows everyone. So the deterrent against speaking up is very strong, and the protection is very weak.

So what would I want? A few things.

First, I think there should be a clearly defined, legally protected channel for employees to raise concerns about AI safety risks — including risks that aren't currently illegal. Something like: if you have a good-faith belief that your company is doing something that poses a serious risk to public safety or national security, you should be able to report that to some designated government body, and you should be protected from retaliation for doing so. The key word is "good-faith" — you shouldn't have to be right, you just have to honestly believe it. Otherwise the standard is too high and nobody will ever use it.

Second, there needs to be some mechanism for the information to actually go somewhere useful. It's not enough to say "you can report it." There has to be a body that has the expertise to evaluate the claim, and the authority to do something about it if it's serious. Right now, if I'd reported a concern in 2023, who would I even have told? Nobody in government had the technical context. That's gradually improving, but it's still a gap.

Third — and this is the part I feel most strongly about — companies shouldn't be able to contract their way around this. No non-disparagement agreements that cover safety concerns. No NDAs that would prevent you from talking to a regulator. And critically, you shouldn't be able to tie someone's equity or severance to their silence. The OpenAI situation got a lot of attention because the terms were so extreme, but I think the general principle matters: if the financial consequences of speaking up are large enough, the protection is meaningless in practice even if it exists on paper.

Fourth, I'd want some kind of protection for talking to the public, not just the government, at least in certain circumstances. This one is harder, because obviously companies have legitimate interests in protecting trade secrets, and you don't want employees just dumping model weights or proprietary techniques on the internet. But there's a difference between "here's how our architecture works" and "our model can do this dangerous thing and we're deploying it anyway." I think there should be a carve-out for the second kind of disclosure, with reasonable guardrails — maybe you have to go through the government channel first and give them some period of time to act, and only if they don't can you go public.

And then fifth, something I think gets underrated: there should be protections for people who stay, not just people who leave. A lot of the discussion is about ex-employees, but the people with the most information are current employees, and they're the ones with the most to lose. So things like: companies can't fire you or demote you or freeze you out of projects because you raised a concern internally, and there's some external body you can go to if you think that's happening.

Now, there's a version of this that I think is dangerously weak and a version I think is too strong. The weak version is what a lot of the companies have voluntarily committed to, which is basically "we promise not to retaliate, trust us." That's not nothing, but it's not enforceable, and the companies can change their policies whenever they want. The too-strong version would be something that lets any disgruntled employee leak anything they want with no consequences, which would be bad both for the companies and honestly for safety — you don't want capabilities proliferating because someone was annoyed about a performance review.

I think the right balance is roughly what I described: a government channel with real teeth, protection from contractual retaliation, and a limited path to public disclosure for genuinely serious stuff. And I'd want this to be federal law, not just company policy, because the whole point is that it has to hold up when the company's interests and the public's interests diverge. That's precisely the situation where the voluntary stuff tends to evaporate.

The last thing I'll say is that I think this matters more than it might seem, because the companies really are the only ones who know what's going on inside them. The government doesn't have access to the models. The public definitely doesn't. So the employees are basically the only check we have right now, and we're currently doing almost nothing to enable them to play that role. If timelines are short — and I think they might be — this is one of the cheapest, most tractable things we could do to improve the situation.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a protected channel for reporting safety risks to a government body, but does not say every employee should know they are legally entitled to discuss company activities privately with government or watchdog agencies.

r002.rationale: It identifies gaps in legal protections for risks that are not illegal, but does not identify employees’ lack of awareness of existing disclosure rights as a protection gap.

astra-6.text:
I’d like employees to have a clear, protected way to raise concerns about serious risks, even when what they’re reporting isn’t obviously illegal. A lot of the things we’re worried about with advanced AI aren’t covered by existing laws. If a company is being reckless, but hasn’t technically broken a law, employees should still be able to tell someone who can do something about it.

That means having an independent body they can report to confidentially, with the technical expertise and access needed to investigate. And it means meaningful protection against retaliation: being fired, being sued for violating a nondisclosure agreement, or losing compensation shouldn’t be the price of raising a good-faith safety concern.

I don’t think that should mean anyone can publish arbitrary confidential information. There should be a process that protects genuinely sensitive information while allowing concerns to get outside the company. The basic principle is that the company shouldn’t have the final say over whether the public gets to learn about a serious risk the company itself is creating.

r001.rationale: The response proposes confidential reporting to an independent body, but does not say every employee should know they are legally entitled to discuss company activities privately with designated agencies.

r002.rationale: It says existing laws do not cover many AI risks; it does not identify employees’ lack of awareness of existing disclosure rights as a protection gap.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want employees to be able to raise concerns about serious risks without having to gamble their careers or their financial security on it. That means protection against retaliation, but it also means making sure that nondisclosure agreements and nondisparagement agreements can’t be used to prevent people from reporting those concerns.

Ideally, there would be a clear channel to an independent government body that has the technical expertise and the authority to investigate. You could go to them with confidential information, and they could actually do something about it. Just saying “You’re allowed to tell a regulator” isn’t enough if there’s no regulator equipped to receive the information.

And I’d want the protections to cover someone who has a reasonable, good-faith concern about a serious danger, even if they can’t prove that the company has broken a law. With AI, a lot of the things we should be worried about might be perfectly legal. We shouldn’t have to wait until something is illegal—or until the harm has already happened—before employees can safely speak up.

r001.rationale: The response supports protected, confidential reporting to an independent government body, but does not say every employee should know they are legally entitled to discuss company activities with designated agencies.

r002.rationale: It identifies the lack of an equipped regulator as a gap, not employees’ lack of awareness of existing disclosure rights.
